content:
Students had the opportunity to test ghost-hunting equipment during the Litowitz Center for Enlightened Disagreement’s ghost tour.

With ghost-hunting equipment and stories of Chicago’s haunted past, Northwestern students and staff traversed campus Thursday evening on a ghost tour hosted by the Litowitz Center for Enlightened Disagreement.

The tour, led by paranormal investigator Tony Szabelski, began in Norris University Center and took students from sites like the Lakefill and The Rock to Kresge Hall and Alice Millar Chapel. 

Many of Szabelski’s stories centered around Sheridan Road, which he said was once notorious for ghost sightings. Prior to the tour, Szabelski distributed electromagnetic readers so the group could detect potential paranormal activity.

“A lot of people go to that theory that spirits are more active in the fall,” Szabelski said. “But my personal belief is more that if there is a spirit at any particular location … it is not going to know time and space the way we do.”

He also showed the group dowsing rods — two L-shaped rods which are traditionally used to point to hidden water sources. Szabelski said that, when the rods cross over each other, they represent a spirit answering paranormal investigators’ questions.

Elisabeth Kamaka, a second-year audiology graduate student, said trying the dowsing rods was her favorite part of the tour, because her results while using them in Kresge Hall courtyard matched with other participants at the location.

“Maybe there’s a water line over there,” she said. “But then that wouldn’t explain why it was pointing to different things when you would ask it stuff.”

Weinberg sophomore Daniel Laguna said he was most curious about Szabelski’s ghostbox — a radio scanner connected to a speaker to attempt real-time communication with ghosts. 

Laguna and other attendees attempted to talk to spirits in front of Alice Millar Chapel by asking the ghostbox questions about the year and whether spirits were trapped in the Chapel’s windows.

Szabelski said not all of his tours yielded the same results because “you can’t make spirits do things on command.”

“I just think supernatural investigation is something really interesting,” Laguna said. “Because of how unknown it remains, the last thing I would want to do would be to dismiss it as pseudoscience.”

The event was part of the Litowitz Center’s inaugural Campus Reading Program, which selected “Vigil,” a novel exploring death and the possibility of absolution.

The Center’s program coordinator, Nick Benson, said the ghost tour aligned with its other programming this quarter, including readathons and a dinner conversation about death.

“It’s done in, we hope, a more fun way,” he said. “(Students) don’t have to like reading at all to enjoy a ghost tour and play with the themes that are discussed in the Campus Reading Program.”

Both Kamaka and Laguna said they had not read “Vigil” but were intrigued by conversations about death and superstitions the ghost tour offered.

Kamaka added she appreciated the intimate feel of the tour, had “no notes” for the guide and enjoyed the stories he shared.

Szabelski, who led an NU ghost tour a few years ago, said he was excited to return to campus because he often thinks about the experience whenever he passes through Evanston.

“I just love doing it,” Szabelski said. “I love interacting with the people (and) seeing their reactions, especially when equipment does things.”

“Vigil” author George Saunders is scheduled to speak at the Campus Reading Program’s keynote event Nov. 19 in Cahn Auditorium.
